blocks.text: We must, however, note that neither the chimpanzee nor the orang-utan was known to the ancient naturalists; there is no mention of them in Aristotle, Pliny or Aelian.
Should read קרד, Arabic قِرْد [qird]
On the double meaning of אריותא see §. 132, appendix.

Rarely, indeed, is so great an accumulation of tropes for designating the divine being found as in the well-known 4th Schir ha-Jichud; there God is compared with נשר, שחל, לביא, ארי, דוב, נמר, עש and כפיר.
A great braggart who has nothing good in mind is called אריא ארבא, “lurking lion” (B. Kama 85a; cf. Ps. 10, 9).

Sanhedrin 102a states: אין ארי דורם נוהם, where the word דורם should probably be deleted. — Ibid. 108b mentions the case in which the lion is said not to kill but rather to nourish itself from the rays of the sun; cf., however, §. 514.

Aelian fell into the opposite error, giving (Thierg. 4, 34) the gestation period of the lioness as 2 months; see, however, the scholia of Fr. Jacobs, who, following Gillius, deletes the words in question and remarks that Philes also assumes that duration of two months.

In our Talmud passage it is related hyperbolically that at the roar of the אריא דבי עילאי the wall of Rome collapsed from a distance of 400 parasangs; similarly it is related in the Jerusalem Talmud B. batra 2, 3 that at the roar of the Persian lions (גורי פרסייא) the wall of the city חמץ collapsed. — Perhaps the proper name is identical with חמת (Gen. 10, 18); see Jonathan on the passage.
Nunc Varias et pardos, qui mares sunt, appellant in eo omni genere cereberrimo in Africa Syriaque (Plin. h. n. 8, 17, 23).
In Midr, Jalk. Schim. part 2, fol. 114, d our animal is called פנתרין.
It was customary to keep for it the blood of the female discharge; yet as a result of its consuming it, a person is said to be weakened (in a magical respect) (Sabbat 75b).
Let it be noted that Buxdorf Lex. p. 2063 translates אפא דיכרא as basilisk. — In the Jerusalem Talmud B. Kama 2b it says: The male hyena (צבוע זכר) is at times as dangerous as the lion (קשה כארי).
The well-known fable of the fox and the grapes, on account of which he starved himself for three days etc., is found in Midr. Rabba Kohelet fol. 98, c.
In Midr. Jalk. Schim. part 2, fol. 122, d the wolf is called אקניתא, i.e., Κνηκίας [Knēkias], “the tawny one,” an epithet of the wolf; the lexica do not explain the word.
This, however, holds only of the pack, for wolves living sociably do not readily attack humans (Arist. l. c. 8, 7, 1).

The Greek Κύων [Kyōn] recurs in קינוניא “hunt” (B. batra 75a), which is compounded of κύων [kyōn] and ἄγω [agō]; from this legendary passage, however, one cannot infer acquaintance with the actual hunting dog (§. 125), since it is mentioned nowhere else in the Talmud.

The Masorah remarks on this biblical passage that נבחו has a רבתי ו"ן, and so the similarity of form gave occasion for confusing the ו with final ן (cf. Geiger in Ozar Nechmad vol. 2, p. 88); this confusion is not rare: thus Elias in the Meturgeman has חוין for חוין (Ps. 126, 6); for גמוז the Aruch reads גמוין. Even initial נ sometimes stands for ו; thus Salomo in the Parchon (s.v. עון) takes the מעוניה occurring in Jes. 23, 11 for מעוזיה. It is probable that originally נבחן, the chald. participial form, was read for נֹבֵחַ, and that the ז arose from ן through confusion; perhaps ארגז can be explained in this way; this word may originally have been ארגן, corresponding to the Latin arcanum (from arca), in the sense that the ארגן served for hiding, storing, concealing, and the ז arose from ן.
The muzzle that is tied onto the wild dog is called סוגר (Jerusalem Talmud Beza C. 2, H. 8).
Cf. p. 24, note*.

It was even called איב “enemy of man” (Jerusalem Talmud Terumoth C. 8, H. 8). — We give here, in passing, some statements of the Midrash about the nature of the dog. Rabba Bereschit fol. 23a says that the dog (like the camel) copulates backwards; ibid. fol. 82, c, that with a flock one, sometimes two sheepdogs are used; ibid. Schemoth fol. 157, c, that the expression כלב חצוף שבחיות is to be understood of its obstinacy; finally, ibid. Echa fol. 60a relates that once lamb's meat had the taste of dog meat; it was investigated and found that the lamb, whose mother had died, had suckled from a bitch. — The Talmudic proverb “A dog does not bark in a strange town for seven years” (Erubin 61a) suggests that this animal feels ill at ease in foreign parts and is afraid of the native companions; on the use of the number seven see §. 438, at the end.

In our Talmud passage the game of chess is called נרדשיר, more correctly in Jehuda ha-Levi (Kusari 5, 20): ארדשיר; this was the name of the Persian king under whom the game of chess is said to have been invented; ארדשיר therefore designates specifically the chess king, while the game of chess is there called מלחמה שטר"נג.

As is well known, great wildness is ascribed to hybrids, cf. article Leopard, at the end, and so the sense in Rabba Echa fol. 63, col. 4 is to be understood when it says there: מעשה בכלבא אחת כופריה שעלהה לראש הסלע ושימשה עם זכר: the hybrid female shrank from no danger in order to satisfy her lust.
In the edition of the Jerusalem Talmud available to me (see appendix), our passage (Schekalim 50, c) has דייתא (vulture) for נמיה.

In this Talmud (not Mishnah) passage it says: שיניה דקות ועקומות; compare with this Raschi (Deut. 32, 5), where it says: בלשון משנה חולדה ששיניה עקומות ועקושות, which probably requires emendation; it is also possible that Raschi had a different reading of our Talmud passage before him.
Mustelarum duo genera; alterum silvestre, distans magnitudine.
